title: Rep. James M. Hoops voted Yea on HB611, a cannabis regulation bill
text:
Rep. James M. Hoops voted Yea on HB611, a cannabis regulation bill
Rep. James M. Hoops (R-81st) voted Yea on HB611, a cannabis regulation bill, which passed the Ohio House 87-5 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and may include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
This bill modifies Ohio’s cannabis laws to grant certain existing medical marijuana processors new cultivation and dispensary opportunities and to integrate them into the adult-use market. It requires the Division of Cannabis Control to issue specified adult-use dispensary, cultivator, processor and testing laboratory licenses to qualifying medical license holders tied to their December 7, 2023, status and ownership structure, and allows up to 40 level III adult-use cultivator and 50 additional adult-use dispensary licenses. The bill authorizes some level III adult-use cultivators to grow and sell medical marijuana, brings them under existing tracking, inspection and enforcement systems, and permits medical processors and labs to obtain products from those cultivators.
HB611 was introduced by Brian Stewart and Jamie Callender.
Hoops is serving his fourth full term in the Ohio House, having been appointed during the 132nd General Assembly. He previously served in the Ohio House from 1999 to 2006 and held the position of Henry County Auditor from 1985 to 1998.
Hoops holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Business and Computer Programming from Northwest State University of Louisiana and is currently the Chair of the House Development Committee for the 136th General Assembly. He has also been elected as the majority whip for the 135th General Assembly and serves on several committees including Commerce and Labor, Community Revitalization, and Finance.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
